books.section: Topic 6.6 The Rise of Industrial Capitalism
America Transformed into the Industrial Giant of the World (1870–1910)
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth” (The Gospel of Wealth), North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text: The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship. The conditions of human life have not only been changed, but revolutionized, within the past few hundred years. In former days there was little difference between the dwelling, dress, food, and environment of the chief and those of his retainers. … The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. But whether the change be for good or ill, it is upon us, beyond our power to alter, and, therefore, to be accepted and made the best of.
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review 148 (June 1889). Public domain; wording and punctuation follow the original North American Review text. Ellipsis marks an omission between complete sentences.

stem: Carnegie says the change is “beyond our power to alter.” What does this show about his view of inequality?

options.text: He accepted great inequality as fixed in modern life
He wanted the government to end inequality at once
options.misconception: Carnegie says the change cannot be altered, so he does not ask government to end it.

options.text: He believed inequality would vanish on its own
options.misconception: Carnegie says the change is here to stay, not that it will vanish.

options.text: He blamed workers for their own poverty
options.misconception: Carnegie blames no one here; he describes a change beyond anyone’s power to alter.

rationales.A: Calling the change beyond our power to alter means accepting it as fixed.
rationales.B: Carnegie does not ask the government to end what he calls unalterable.
rationales.C: Carnegie says the change is upon us to stay, not that it will vanish.
rationales.D: Carnegie describes the change, he does not blame workers for it.
rationales.general:
Take Carnegie’s sentence at its word.
1. Carnegie says the change is upon us, for good or ill.
2. He adds that it is beyond our power to alter.
3. What cannot be altered must be accepted and made the best of.
4. Background from the books: Carnegie paired his acceptance of inequality with a duty to give wealth away.
Remember: when an author calls something unalterable, the author is accepting it.
